items.prompt: What does skin make when sunlight falls on it?

options.label: Vitamin D
options.feedback: A fat in the skin absorbs the UV and is rearranged into it.

options.label: Calcium
options.feedback: Calcium comes from food and is absorbed in the gut. Skin does not build minerals out of light.

options.label: Melanin
options.feedback: Melanin is made in response to UV, but it is a shield the skin builds, not a product carried to the rest of the body.

options.label: Keratin
options.feedback: Keratin is the protein that toughens skin, hair and nails, and it is made constantly, with or without sun.

items.ok_line: Sunlight is a factory switch for skin.
items.ko_line: One of these is built directly from a UV ray hitting a fat molecule in the skin.
items.exp_text: A form of cholesterol sits in the skin's outer layers, and UV light striking it breaks open one of its rings. The broken molecule then folds into a new shape, and the liver and kidneys finish converting it into the active form the body uses. That reshaped molecule is vitamin D.

items.prompt: What job does melanin do in the skin?

options.label: It absorbs UV light before it reaches deeper cells
options.feedback: It sits above the cells that divide and soaks up the radiation meant for them.

options.label: It cools the skin in hot weather
options.feedback: Cooling the skin is the job of sweat evaporating, not of a pigment sitting in the outer layers.

options.label: It closes the pores against water loss
options.feedback: Pores are closed by other structures entirely; melanin does not seal anything.

options.label: It kills bacteria on the skin's surface
options.feedback: Bacteria on skin are dealt with by sweat's acidity and by the immune system, not by a pigment.

items.ok_line: A pigment that stands between the ray and the cell.
items.ko_line: Melanin is dark, and dark things in nature are usually there to catch light rather than to cool, seal or kill.
items.exp_text: Melanin is a dark pigment packed into grains and pushed up into the skin's surface layers, right above the cells that divide to replace old skin. Because it is dark, it absorbs a wide range of light, including the UV that can damage the DNA inside those dividing cells. It absorbs UV light before it reaches them.

items.prompt: What in the eye tells the body's internal clock what time it is?

options.label: The lens changing shape
options.feedback: The lens changes shape to focus near and far objects. It carries no signal about the clock.

options.label: The colour of what is being looked at
options.feedback: Colour is sorted by the cells used for seeing shapes and hues, a separate path from the clock's.

options.label: Tears keeping the surface moist
options.feedback: Tears protect and lubricate the eye's surface. They carry no light signal anywhere.

options.label: Light striking cells at the back of the eye
options.feedback: A separate set of light-sensing cells reports brightness straight to the brain's clock.

items.ok_line: A second kind of light-sensing cell, built only to report the time of day.
items.ko_line: The clock does not care what is being looked at, only whether light is present.
items.exp_title: A second set of eyes for time, not shape
items.exp_text: Alongside the cells that build the image you see, the retina holds a separate set of cells that do not contribute to that picture at all. They simply report how much light is present, and a direct nerve path carries that report to a small cluster of brain cells that acts as the body's clock. It is that light striking the retina's cells which tells the clock what time it is.

items.prompt: What does the body release into the blood once it grows dark?

options.label: Adrenaline
options.feedback: Adrenaline rises with alertness and stress, and darkness on its own does not trigger it.

options.label: Melatonin
options.feedback: A gland deep in the brain releases it once the eye's light signal drops away.

options.label: Insulin
options.feedback: Insulin is released after eating, to manage blood sugar, and has no link to the light-dark cycle.

options.label: Vitamin D
options.feedback: Vitamin D is built by daylight striking the skin. Darkness prompts no release of it at all.

items.ok_line: The dark itself is the signal.
items.ko_line: Ask which of these four rises specifically because light has gone, not because of stress, food or sun.
items.exp_text: As long as the retina reports daylight, a small gland deep in the brain is held back and stays quiet. Once that light signal drops away at nightfall, the gland is released from that restraint and starts pouring its hormone into the blood. What it releases once it grows dark is melatonin.

items.prompt: Why does the pupil grow smaller in bright light?

options.label: To keep dust from entering the eye
options.feedback: Dust is kept out by eyelashes and blinking, not by the size of the pupil.

options.label: To sharpen the lens for close reading
options.feedback: Focusing for near or far is done by the lens changing shape, a separate muscle system from the pupil's.

options.label: To limit how much light reaches the retina
options.feedback: A ring of muscle closes the opening so fewer rays get through to the light-sensing cells behind it.

options.label: To cool the surface of the eye
options.feedback: The pupil has no role in temperature; its opening only controls how much light passes through.

items.ok_line: A smaller opening, a smaller flood of light.
items.ko_line: The pupil is only an opening. Ask what passing through an opening lets through more or less of.
items.exp_title: A dimmer switch made of muscle
items.exp_text: The coloured ring around the pupil is a muscle, and in bright light it contracts inward, narrowing the opening at its centre. A narrower opening lets fewer rays pass through to the retina behind it, protecting those light-sensing cells from being overwhelmed. The pupil shrinks to limit how much light reaches the retina.

items.prompt: Why can you not see colour in a dimly lit room?

options.label: Because colour needs the lens to bend light more sharply
options.feedback: The lens bends light to focus an image, the same job whether the room is bright or dim. It plays no part in sensing colour.

options.label: Because the cells that sense colour need bright light to work
options.feedback: Those cells respond weakly to dim light, leaving only the cells built for low light active.

options.label: Because the pupil closes and blocks colour specifically
options.feedback: In dim light the pupil opens wider to let in more light of every kind; it does not filter colour out.

options.label: Because the brain switches off colour to save energy
options.feedback: Nothing is switched off in the brain. The limit sits earlier, in which retinal cells are receiving enough light to respond.

items.ok_line: The colour cells are simply not getting enough light to fire.
items.ko_line: Two kinds of cell sense light in the retina, and only one of them needs plenty of it.
items.exp_title: One set of cells needs more light than the other
items.exp_text: The retina holds two kinds of light-sensing cell: cone cells, which detect colour but only respond well once light is fairly bright, and rod cells, which detect no colour at all but respond even to a faint glow. In dim light there is not enough for the cone cells to fire, so only the colourless rod cells are sending a signal. Colour drops out because the cells that sense it need bright light to work.

items.prompt: Why does going from a dark room into bright sunlight cause a flash of pain?

options.label: Because the pupil is still wide open from the dark
options.feedback: It had opened wide to catch what little light there was, and it takes a moment to narrow again.

options.label: Because the lens has not yet adjusted its shape
options.feedback: The lens focuses distance, not brightness, and its adjustment causes no pain of this kind.

options.label: Because the eye has run out of tears
options.feedback: Tear supply has nothing to do with how much light enters the eye.

options.label: Because melanin has not yet reached the eye's surface
options.feedback: Melanin sits in the coloured iris and deeper layers already, well before any change in light; it is not delivered on demand.

items.ok_line: A wide opening built for the dark, suddenly flooded.
items.ko_line: Think about the size of the opening the eye had set for near-darkness a moment earlier.
items.exp_title: A gate too wide for the moment
items.exp_text: In a dark room the pupil widens as far as it can, admitting every scrap of available light. Stepping into sunlight floods that same wide opening with far more light than it was set for, and the sudden overload of the retina registers as a stab of pain until the muscle ring narrows it back down. The flash of pain happens because the pupil is still wide open from the dark.

items.prompt: Why does pale skin turn red and sore after too much sun?

options.label: Because sweat glands become blocked
options.feedback: Sweat glands play no part here; the redness sits in the skin's blood vessels and cells, not its ducts.

options.label: Because UV light damages skin cells and blood flow increases to repair them
options.feedback: The blood carries in the cells and materials needed to clear away the damage, and that extra blood is what shows as red.

options.label: Because the skin loses its layer of melanin
options.feedback: Sun exposure prompts the skin to build more melanin over following days, not less, and burning happens before that extra pigment can form.

options.label: Because salt from sweat irritates the skin
options.feedback: Sunburn happens on skin that never sweated at all, such as on a cool but sunny day, so salt is not the cause.

items.ok_line: Redness is the repair crew arriving, not the injury itself.
items.ko_line: The pain and colour of a sunburn are signs of the body responding, not of something clogging or draining the skin.
items.exp_text: UV light striking the skin's outer cells can break the DNA inside them, and cells with damage they cannot repair are marked for removal. That marking triggers inflammation, which widens the small blood vessels near the surface so more blood, carrying immune cells, can reach the site. The extra blood flow shows through the skin as the red, sore patch, because UV light damaged the cells and blood flow rose to deal with it.

items.prompt: Why do people with dark skin need longer sun exposure to make the same amount of vitamin D as people with pale skin?

options.label: Their skin absorbs less UV light because melanin blocks it first
options.feedback: The melanin that shields deeper cells from UV also intercepts the same rays that would otherwise reach the vitamin-making molecule.

options.label: Their skin makes vitamin D from a different molecule
options.feedback: The starting molecule and the whole chemical pathway are the same in every skin tone; only how much UV gets through to it differs.

options.label: Their skin has fewer sweat glands
options.feedback: Sweat gland number does not vary by skin tone in a way that matters here, and sweat plays no role in making vitamin D.

options.label: Their liver processes vitamin D more slowly
options.feedback: The liver's part of the process is the same regardless of skin tone; the difference happens earlier, at the skin's surface.

items.ok_line: The same pigment that shields also shades the vitamin-making molecule.
items.ko_line: The chemistry inside the skin is identical across skin tones; only the amount of UV reaching it differs.
items.exp_title: A shield that shades both ways
items.exp_text: Melanin absorbs UV light to protect the DNA in dividing skin cells, but that same absorption competes with the molecule lower in the skin that needs UV to become vitamin D. In skin with more melanin, more of the incoming UV is caught by the pigment before it can reach that molecule, so fewer conversions happen per minute of sun. Longer exposure is needed because their skin absorbs less UV light, melanin having blocked it first.

items.prompt: Why does working night shifts under electric light for years tend to disrupt sleep and health?

options.label: Electric light is too dim for the eye to focus properly
options.feedback: Focusing is unaffected by shift work; the lens adjusts to any workable brightness. The problem lies elsewhere.

options.label: The body's clock keeps reading light and dark at the wrong hours
options.feedback: Bright light at night and darkness by day repeatedly send the clock signals that contradict the actual time.

options.label: Melanin builds up without sunlight to clear it away
options.feedback: Melanin is not cleared by sunlight and does not accumulate from a lack of it; it has no bearing on sleep.

options.label: The lens of the eye cannot process artificial light
options.feedback: The eye responds to light regardless of its source; a photon from a bulb signals the clock exactly as one from the sun would.

items.ok_line: The clock trusts whatever light pattern it is shown, day after day.
items.ko_line: The eye reads light the same way regardless of its source; the trouble is in when that light arrives.
items.exp_title: A clock fed the wrong pattern
items.exp_text: The brain's clock sets itself using nothing but the pattern of light and dark reported by the retina, with no way to know whether that light comes from the sun or a bulb. A night shift under bright electric light, followed by sleep behind curtains by day, repeatedly shows the clock a pattern that runs opposite to the true day-night cycle. Health and sleep suffer because the body's clock keeps reading light and dark at the wrong hours.
